case_studies.title: Honeyval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for LLM-powered HTTP Honeypots
case_studies.abstract: Honeypots are decoy systems mimicking real system components designed to defend against cyber attacks. Recently, LLMs increasingly serve as simulation backbones for honeypots. They enable defenders to construct high-interaction honeypots with low system security risks. However, LLM-powered honeypot development lacks a unified evaluation framework. Most evaluations consist of measuring response similarity on fixed commands, manual testing, or real-world deployment. These methods are often not scalable for development, reproducible across evaluations, representative of practical attacks, or adap
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating LLM-powered HTTP honeypots by building a comprehensive evaluation framework called Honeyval, which resulted in a more scalable and reproducible way to test these honeypots. The framework allows for more efficient development and deployment of LLM-powered honeypots. This can help improve defence against cyber attacks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure with LLM-powered HTTP honeypots, consider using the Honeyval framework to evaluate and improve your honeypot's effectiveness. Check your current evaluation methods to see if they are scalable and reproducible. This can help you strengthen your organisation's defence against cyber attacks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High IT relevance as it directly affects how IT engineers work with LLMs and honeypots. Novel evaluation frameworks are valuable for building and improving honeypot systems (high Novelty and Value 90 Days). Purely academic novelty is low (5), but the IT relevance makes up for it.

case_studies.title: Do Proactive Agents Really Need an LLM to Decide When to Wake and What to Anchor?
case_studies.abstract: Proactive agents read user activity as text and call an LLM on every event to decide whether to act. But user activity is not natively text: it is a structured event stream of (actor, verb, object, timestamp) tuples that the operating system already maintains in graph form. Rendering the structure as text and asking an LLM to recover it is a round-trip the system never had to take. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of proactive agents needing a large language model to decide when to take action, by building a smaller temporal-graph-learning model that uses graph updates instead of text. The result is a more efficient way to trigger actions based on user activity. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving the efficiency of proactive agents using graph updates rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper has moderate novelty because it reveals a surprising aspect of proactive agents and their interaction with LLMs. It has high IT relevance because it directly affects how proactive agents and LLMs interact. It has high value because it provides a specific and actionable way to decide when to wake and what to anchor proactive agents without using an LLM. IT engineers could use this to optimize proactive agent systems within 90 days.

case_studies.title: GenClaw: Code-Driven Agentic Image Generation
case_studies.abstract: Image generation models have evolved from text-conditioned pixel synthesis toward multimodal agents endowed with visual comprehension and tool invocation capabilities. Yet, existing agents remain at the mercy of underlying black-box image models. Their workflow is trapped in a repetitive cycle of prompt rewriting for generation refinement, leaving them with no mechanism to directly manipulate the canvas. In essence, the potential of LLMs to serve as a genuine "brush" for precise visual construction remains largely untapped. In this paper, we propose GenClaw, a code-driven agentic image generat
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited control in image generation models by introducing GenClaw, a code-driven agentic image generation model. The authors built GenClaw to provide direct manipulation of the canvas, allowing for more precise visual construction. The result is a more controllable and refined image generation process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on image generation models and their potential applications in creative fields.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: 15 (LLMs with visual manipulation capabilities is an emerging area and could appeal to some engineers), IT Relevance: 18 (code-driven agentic image generation relates to LLM APIs but is quite niche), Value: 7 (while it could spark some research or interest in code-driven image generation, its practical use in IT infrastructure or real-world impact is low).

case_studies.title: LLMSurgeon: Diagnosing Data Mixture of Large Language Models
case_studies.abstract: The pretraining data mixture of Large Language Models (LLMs) constitutes their "digital DNA", shaping model behaviors, capabilities, and failure modes. Yet this composition is rarely disclosed, making post-hoc auditing of data combination or provenance difficult. In this work, we formalize $\textbf{Data Mixture Surgery (DMS)}$: given only generated text from a target LLM, estimate the domain-level distribution of its pretraining corpus under a predefined taxonomy. We propose $\textbf{LLMSurgeon}$, a strong framework that casts DMS as an inverse problem under the label-shift assumption. Rather
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of identifying the pretraining data mixture of Large Language Models, by building a framework called LLMSurgeon that can estimate the domain-level distribution of the pretraining corpus. The result is a tool that can help audit and understand the data combination of these models. This research does not directly affect cloud infrastructure management work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on auditing Large Language Models rather than managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper introduces a framework for auditing the pretraining data of Large Language Models (LLMs), which is relevant to IT engineers working with LLM APIs. The novelty is moderate, and the paper does not directly impact how IT engineers work, but the concept of data mixture surgery could be useful in identifying biases in LLMs used for SaaS applications. The value to IT engineers or consultants lies in understanding the data composition of LLMs they deploy, but this may not directly lead to actions or automation within 90 days.

case_studies.title: EASE Configuration Facilitates A Reproducible Science of LLM Social Simulations
case_studies.abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed to simulate social interactions, yet many of the existing simulators remain ad hoc and monolithic. This lack of architectural standardization prevents reproducible research and complicates downstream evaluation. We advance a rigorous science of LLM-based multi-agent simulation by modularizing core components into Environments, Agents, Simulation engines, and Evaluation metrics (EASE). case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of reproducing science in Large Language Model (LLM) social simulations by creating a modular framework called EASE. The EASE configuration modularizes core components, allowing for more standardized and reproducible research. The result is a more rigorous science of LLM-based simulations.
